title: When Competitors Force You to Cannibalize Yourself
documentTitle: AdWords Cross-Exchange Buying Update — Project AwBid Status Email
excerptForBlog: Welcome to the first of several updates on the status of project "AwBid" enabling cross exchange buying in AdWords. We'll be sending out these updates throughout this year as we hit our major milestones. What is AwBid? AwBid is a project to enable AdWords buyers to access additional inventory outside of the traditional AdSense and Ad Exchange publishers. Through AwBid, buyers in AdWords will have access to Yahoo! owned and operated content, Windows Live and Hotmail content (via AppNexus) as well as inventory available on many third party ad exchanges such as AdMeld, PubMatic, Rubicon and adBrite. The goal is to integrate the new inventory sources as seamlessly as possible into AdWords. We are working on a very aggressive timeline for this project as many of our competitors are already offering a similar feature. We understand that many of you have concerns about how this will affect other parts of our business, particularly AdX and AdSense. The AWBid team is working closely with the product managers for our display business (GDN, Invite, AdX, and AdSense) to understand the strategic implications of this effort and how to manage them thoughtfully. We don't plan to launch this change just yet. We will make sure we've worked through the strategic questions and have everyone on board before we do.

lessonTitle: When Competitors Force You to Cannibalize Yourself
pullQuote: If rivals are already selling what you fear to build, the only thing worse than disrupting your own business is letting them do it for you.
situation: In February 2011, a Google product manager named Zachary Goldberg sent an update email about 'Project AwBid' — a plan to let AdWords buyers purchase ad inventory from outside Google's own networks, including Yahoo, Hotmail, and third-party exchanges like PubMatic and Rubicon. The email explicitly flags that the project could cannibalize Google's own AdX and AdSense businesses. It was written to a broad internal audience, framed as the first in a series of milestone updates.
insight: The hidden move here isn't the product decision — it's the internal politics of launching something that threatens your own revenue streams. Goldberg writes that Google is on 'a very aggressive timeline' because 'many of our competitors are already offering a similar feature.' That's a classic competitive-response signal: the market is setting the clock, not internal comfort. But the email also admits the team 'don't plan to launch this change just yet' and will 'work through the strategic questions' first. That's not hesitation — it's deliberate sequencing. Build the product, then secure internal alignment before you ship. The risk Google is managing is classic platform cannibalization: opening AdWords to outside inventory could pull spend away from AdSense and AdX, products Google also owns. By naming that tension explicitly and assigning product managers to study it, leadership is treating the conflict as a solvable coordination problem, not a reason to kill the project.
application: If your next product move puts two of your own revenue lines in competition, don't bury that conflict in a footnote. Name it in the kickoff document, assign someone to own the coordination problem, and sequence your launch so internal stakeholders are aligned before customers ever see it. A surprise cannibalization event inside your company is far more disruptive than the competitive pressure that made the move necessary.
